title: Tips For Maximising Returns On Mutual Fund
summary: Choose a mutual fund by your goal and its date, then the category, the risk, and a few checks on record, costs, exit load and fund manager.
body_markdown:
Start with what the money is for and when you will need it, not with a fund's name. That date points you to a kind of fund, which SEBI calls a category. Within the category you compare a few funds on their risk, their record against the benchmark, their costs and their exit terms.


## How do you choose a mutual fund?


You choose in six steps, in this order.


1. **Name the goal and its date.** A down payment in two years and retirement in twenty-five need different funds.
2. **Count the time you have.** The years left decide which kinds of fund make sense.
3. **Check the risk you can sit through.** The riskometer, SEBI's six-level risk label, shows how risky each fund is.
4. **Pick the category.** This is the kind of fund, such as large cap or short duration.
5. **Compare funds inside it.** Look at record, costs, exit terms and the manager.
6. **Decide how you will pay.** Either a lump sum (a larger amount at one time) or a SIP (a fixed amount at regular intervals).


How many funds you need is covered in[mutual fund diversification](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-diversification) .


## Which mutual fund is best?


No single fund is best for everyone, because a fund is good or poor for a particular job.


SEBI sorts funds into categories so that funds of the same kind follow the same rules at every fund house. A large cap fund from one fund house must invest the way a large cap fund from any other does. That lets you compare like with like.


For "which fund", go to the lists on our category pages. They rank funds by their three-year return and show the category's average 1-, 3- and 5-year returns, counting only funds with at least three years of history. These are past figures, not a forecast. Start at[mutual fund categories](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories) , or see[flexi cap funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/flexi-cap-funds) for one example.


## How does your goal decide the kind of fund?


The time before you need the money decides the kind of fund. Koshex suggests these pairings, and they come from[our category hub](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories) , not from SEBI.


Time before you need the money Categories Koshex suggests looking at


Days to a few months Overnight, liquid


Up to 1 year Money market, ultra short


1 to 3 years Short duration, corporate bond, banking and PSU


3 to 5 years Balanced hybrid, dynamic asset allocation, equity savings


5 years or more Large cap, flexi cap, aggressive hybrid


For seven years or more, the hub also lists mid cap, small cap and multi cap.


Three situations show it.


- **A flat down payment due in about two years.** That sits in the one-to-three-year row, which points to categories such as[short duration funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/short-duration-funds) .
- **Retirement twenty-five years away.** That is longer than the five- and seven-year rows, so those categories are open. Your comfort with a fall then decides which.
- **Tax saving each March under the old tax regime.** The category is ELSS. It has a three-year lock-in (a period when you cannot sell) from the allotment of each purchase, so every SIP instalment is locked separately. The deduction is under section 123 (the old Section 80C), up to ₹1,50,000 a year across all eligible items, under the old regime only. See[ELSS funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/elss-funds) .


## What should you check before you pick a fund?


Once the category is fixed, check five things you can read yourself. To compare two funds, put them side by side in the same category and read the same line for each.


### The riskometer and the label


The riskometer is the risk label SEBI makes every fund show, on six levels from Low to Very High. Fund houses reassess it every month and disclose it within 10 calendar days of month-end, and a change is sent to the scheme's unitholders.


You find it on the front page of the application form and the scheme document, with the benchmark's riskometer beside it. On 29 September 2026, every flexi cap fund on our category pages read Very High, and most short duration funds there read Moderate.


Because it can change, a fund's risk can move after you buy. For what the levels mean, read[the risks in mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/what-are-risks-involved-in-mutual-funds) .


### The benchmark and the past record


A benchmark is the index a fund measures itself against. Fund houses must compare a scheme with the total return version of its benchmark index, which counts dividends as well as price changes. SEBI asks for a first benchmark that reflects the category, such as the BSE 100 or NSE 100 index for a large cap fund.


AMFI's website shows each fund's return as CAGR, the average yearly growth rate as if the fund had grown at the same pace every year. It covers 1, 3, 5 and 10 years and since launch, next to the benchmark's. Adverts also show what ₹10,000 invested would have become. See[absolute return vs CAGR](https://koshex.com/blog/absolute-return-vs-cagr) , and[five ways to measure mutual fund risk](https://koshex.com/blog/5-ways-to-measure-mutual-fund-risk) for the risk numbers beside them.


### Costs


The expense ratio is the fund's yearly fee, shown as a percentage of your money and taken out of the fund's value. SEBI sets a ceiling on the base part of it, and the ceiling falls as the fund grows. For active equity-oriented schemes (mostly invested in shares) it starts at 2.10% on the first ₹500 crore of net assets and falls to 0.95% on the balance.


Here is what a gap in costs does. These rates are made up, and taking the fee off the return is a simplification. Say ₹5,00,000 is invested for 15 years at an assumed 11% a year before costs. With 1.2% a year in costs, the net rate is 9.8% and it ends at ₹20,32,381. With 2.0%, the net rate is 9.0% and it ends at ₹18,21,241. The difference is ₹2,11,140. Try the[lumpsum calculator](https://koshex.com/calculators/lumpsum-calculator) .


Every fund's expense ratio is published daily on the fund house's website and on AMFI's. If the fund house raises it, you get an email or SMS at least three working days before. No scheme charges an entry load, a fee for buying. More in[what the expense ratio is](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-expense-ratio-and-why-is-it-important) .


### Exit load and lock-in


An exit load is a fee some funds charge if you sell within a set time after buying. It is taken out of the price you receive, and for an open-ended scheme it cannot exceed 3% of NAV. NAV is the price of one unit of a fund.


Apart from the few loads SEBI sets itself, such as for liquid funds, each scheme sets its own in its scheme document. One scheme document charges 1% on units redeemed (sold) within 3 months from the date of allotment and nothing after. Another charges 1% before 365 days from the date of allotment. A third lists none.


### The fund manager and the fund house


The scheme document names the fund manager, how long they have run the fund and the other funds they manage. A change of manager is not treated by SEBI as a change in the fund's basic features, so no free exit window opens. See[what to do when a fund manager exits](https://koshex.com/blog/what-to-do-when-a-fund-manager-exits) .


Category rules are the same at every fund house, and so is the trust structure that holds your money.


### Where to read all this


Every scheme's portfolio is disclosed monthly on the fund house's website and AMFI's. Each fund house's website dashboard shows AUM, expense ratios, portfolio and past performance. Most fund houses also publish a factsheet for each fund every month;[five ways to measure mutual fund risk](https://koshex.com/blog/5-ways-to-measure-mutual-fund-risk) shows how to read one.


## Should you pick the fund with the highest recent return?


No. A recent return tells you what happened, and it does not tell you what comes next. AMFI's own wording for illustrations is that "past performance may or may not be sustained in future".


One year says little about a fund built for five. Compare instead within the category, against the benchmark, over several periods, and next to the risk the fund took to get there.


The rules point the same way. SEBI's Advertisement Code bars statements based on assumption or projection, and bars any ranking in a fund house's adverts.


Buying when the market is at a high is a timing question, covered in[when to invest a lump sum or SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/when-is-the-right-time-to-invest-in-lump-sum-and-sip) . Chasing winners is covered in[common behavioural biases](https://koshex.com/blog/common-behavioural-biases-investors-must-avoid) . A low NAV is no bargain either; see[how important NAV is](https://koshex.com/blog/how-important-is-nav-when-choosing-mutual-funds) . A new fund offer has no record to check, as[what is an NFO](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-an-nfo) explains.


## How do you choose a fund for a SIP?


You choose it the same way as for a lump sum, because a SIP is a way of paying into a fund, not a kind of fund. A SIP has no interest rate. Each instalment buys units at that day's NAV, so the value moves with the NAV and can end below what you put in. Each instalment is a separate purchase with its own allotment date and holding period, the time you have owned the unit.


Paying by SIP spreads your purchases, but it does not protect you from a fall in NAV.


Some funds take SIPs from as little as ₹100, and others ask for more, so check the fund you pick. For amounts, see[how much to invest every month](https://koshex.com/blog/how-much-should-i-invest-in-mutual-funds-every-month) . Also read[what a SIP is](https://koshex.com/blog/systematic-investment-plan-sip) and[whether a SIP is safe](https://koshex.com/blog/is-sip-safe) .


## How can you get better returns from the fund you choose?


No secret fund does it. You can influence cost, time and how often you trade.


- **Keep costs in view.** The ₹2,11,140 gap above came from 0.8 percentage points a year.
- **Give the fund time.** See[the power of compounding](https://koshex.com/blog/power-of-compounding-meaning-benefits-working) .
- **Selling and switching often costs money.** Units of an equity-oriented fund sold within 12 months are taxed at 20% as short-term gains, and an exit load may apply too.
- **Review rather than chase.** Koshex reviews your holdings over time and flags changes, such as a fund's category, risk or ranking shifting. See[when to sell a mutual fund](https://koshex.com/blog/when-should-you-sell-a-mutual-fund) .
- **Step up as income grows.** See[step-up SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/step-up-sip) .
- **Rebalancing.** Rebalancing means bringing your mix of funds back to the one you planned; see[how to rebalance](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-rebalance-your-mutual-fund-portfolio) .


If you do change funds, Koshex customers can switch between schemes of the same fund house on Koshex. Koshex also talks you through sharp market falls before you redeem (sell). See[how to switch mutual fund schemes](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-switch-mutual-fund-schemes) .


On tax, here is the short version. An equity-oriented fund holds at least 65% in shares of domestic companies listed in India, on the annual average. Gains on its units sold within 12 months are taxed at 20%. Gains on units held longer are taxed at 12.5% on the amount above ₹1,25,000 in a tax year, one allowance per person across all equity funds and listed shares.


A Specified Mutual Fund has more than 65% in debt and money market instruments. Gains on its units bought on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at your income-tax slab rate, however long you hold them. Full detail is in[how SIP returns are taxed](https://koshex.com/blog/how-sip-returns-are-taxed) .
